title: The elephant head
hookLine: Shiva brings the boy back with an elephant's head and promises he'll be worshipped first
tomorrow: two brothers race around the world. how does the slow one win?

cards: Every family has a story two relatives tell differently, each sure the other got it wrong. Ganesha's head is one of those, and here the relatives are old texts. Here's the Shiva Purana's telling.
Go north, Shiva tells his ganas. Bring back the head of the first living creature you meet. They run down the mountain into the forests, and the first creature they find is an elephant.

Shiva sets its head on the boy's body and breathes life into him. The boy opens his eyes for the second time in his life, and his mother is there again. Now he has a trunk, wide ears, and the face you already know.

teach.b: Now the debate, and it's a real one among people who love him. Why an elephant? One side says: the text's answer is plain.

teach.h: ONE SIDE: THE FIRST CREATURE MET.
teach.b: It was the first creature they met. The head is chance, and the point of the story is what Shiva does next.
The other side says: look at that face. Big ears, to listen more than he speaks. A trunk that can uproot a tree or pick up one grain of rice.
An elephant doesn't go around the forest; it walks through and makes a path. That fits a remover of obstacles too well to shrug off.

And the texts don't even agree on how the head was lost: in the Brahmavaivarta Purana, it happens when Shani, the god of the planet Saturn, looks at the baby. The tradition keeps both tellings side by side.
What they share is the ending. Shiva makes the boy leader of the ganas, the very guards who fought him: Ganesha, Ganapati, lord of the ganas.
And he promises the boy will be worshipped first, before any god, before any ceremony.
That promise is why Hindus begin with Ganesha: a wedding, a housewarming, a new business, even a child's first day of school often starts with a prayer to him. The newest god goes first.

how: Many Hindus begin weddings, housewarmings, new ventures and other ceremonies by honoring Ganesha first, often with a short prayer or mantra to him before anything else begins.

o: an elephant spirit said to guard temple doors in the north
a title of Shiva as lord of the mountain and its forests
lord of the ganas, the elephant-headed god worshipped first

games.q: two sides, one story — tap the pairs.
p: ears that listen, a trunk that clears

s: Ganesha goes first because he's the oldest god
he's the newest. in the story, first place is Shiva's promise to the boy he brought back.
every text tells the head story the same way
the Shiva Purana and the Brahmavaivarta Purana tell it differently, and the tradition keeps both.
Ganesha ends up leading the very guards who fought him
Ganapati, Ganesha: lord of the ganas.

games.q: your cousin says the elephant face means nothing: the text just says it was the first creature they met. what's the best case for the other side?
o: the Shiva Purana itself explains what the ears and trunk mean.
the face fits a remover of obstacles: ears that listen, a trunk that clears a path.
the ganas picked an elephant on purpose, as the strongest animal.
games.why: the text says first creature met; the ears-and-trunk readings come from devotion, not the verse. a good steelman keeps both: chance in the text, meaning in the face.

practice: Think of one thing you're about to begin: today's work, a hard conversation, a trip. Before you start it, pause. Many Hindus say a short line to Ganesha here, like Om Gam Ganapataye Namah, or simply Shri Ganesh.
If you pray, say it quietly three times. If you don't, name the beginning out loud and ask for a clear path.

wordCard.voice: Ganesha: lord of the ganas. The boy who fought the guards ends up leading them, with an elephant's face and first place at every beginning.

orig.note: Sanskrit: elephant (gaja) face (anana), one of Ganesha's names.

carryVoice: Your line: Ganesha first, before every beginning. Shiva's promise to the boy at the door. That's day twenty-four.
